es.summary: Aumento del pH sanguíneo por disminución de PaCO₂ debido a hiperventilación. Puede ser aguda o crónica.
key_points: pH > 7.45 y PaCO₂ < 35 mmHg en gases arteriales.
Causas comunes: ansiedad, dolor, fiebre, sepsis, insuficiencia respiratoria.
Compensación renal disminuye HCO₃⁻, pero es lenta.
Puede producir hipocalemia, hipocalcemia y vasoconstricción cerebral.
El tratamiento se centra en corregir la causa y controlar la ventilación.

pathophysiology: Menor CO₂ reduce la concentración de ácido carbónico, elevando el pH.
Los riñones intentan compensar excretando HCO₃⁻, pero tardan horas‑días.
risk_factors: Hipoxia, insuficiencia cardíaca o enfermedad pulmonar obstructiva.
signs_symptoms: Respiración rápida y profunda (respiración de Kussmaul).
Entumecimiento y hormigueo en manos y cara.
Mareos, confusión o convulsiones en casos graves.
diagnostics: Gases arteriales: pH 7.46‑7.55, PaCO₂ <35 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ normal o ligeramente bajo.
Oxígeno arterial (PaO₂) normalmente normal o elevado.
ECG: puede mostrar arritmias por hipocalemia.
treatment: Identificar y tratar la causa subyacente (ansiedad, dolor, fiebre).
Técnicas de respiración controlada (respiración con labios fruncidos).
Reemplazo de electrolitos: potasio y calcio por vía oral o IV según necesidad.
Oxígeno suplementario solo si hay hipoxemia.
complications: Vasoconstricción cerebral → disminución del flujo sanguíneo y posible síncope.
Descompensación respiratoria si la causa subyacente empeora.
nursing_care: Monitorear gases arteriales cada 2‑4 h hasta estabilización.
Evaluar signos de desequilibrio electrolítico (ECG, debilidad muscular).
Enseñar respiración lenta y profunda; posición semi‑Fowler.
Registrar frecuencia respiratoria, ritmo cardíaco y saturación de O₂.
Administrar reposición de K⁺/Ca²⁺ según indicación médica.
patient_teaching: Practicar técnicas de respiración diafragmática para evitar hiperventilación.
Reconocer síntomas de desequilibrio electrolítico y buscar ayuda.
Mantener hidratación adecuada y seguir dieta rica en potasio (plátano, papaya).
Informar al profesional de salud sobre episodios de ansiedad o dolor intenso.

outcomes: NOC: Equilibrio electrolítico – mantener K⁺ ≥3.5 mEq/L
NOC: Estado neurológico – ausencia de parestesias

interventions.action: Monitorear niveles séricos de K⁺ y Ca²⁺ cada 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Detectar rápidamente desequilibrios que pueden causar arritmias.

interventions.action: Administrar suplementos de potasio o calcio según prescripción.
interventions.rationale: Corregir la hipocalemia/hypocalcemia y prevenir complicaciones.

interventions.action: Evaluar ECG al menos una vez al día o si aparecen palpitaciones.
interventions.rationale: Identificar arritmias relacionadas con alteraciones electrolíticas.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de respiración controlada.
interventions.rationale: Reducir la hiperventilación y la pérdida de CO₂.

outcomes: NOC: Tolerancia a la actividad – paciente completa actividades de la vida diaria sin disnea
NOC: Fatiga – puntuación de escala de fatiga ≤2/10

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de actividad y registrar signos vitales antes y después.
interventions.rationale: Establecer línea base y detectar deterioro.

interventions.action: Planificar períodos de descanso cada 10‑15 min durante actividades.
Aplicar técnicas de respiración diafragmática durante el esfuerzo.
interventions.rationale: Mejorar ventilación y reducir sensación de falta de aire.

interventions.action: Colaborar con fisioterapia para programa de ejercicios graduados.
interventions.rationale: Incrementar gradualmente la capacidad aeróbica y la tolerancia.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de evitar hiperventilación durante el ejercicio.
interventions.rationale: Mantener PaCO₂ dentro de rangos normales y prevenir alcalosis.

en.summary: Increase in blood pH due to decreased PaCO₂ from hyperventilation. Can be acute or chronic.
key_points: pH > 7.45 and PaCO₂ < 35 mmHg in arterial blood gases.
Common causes: anxiety, pain, fever, sepsis, respiratory failure.
Renal compensation decreases HCO₃⁻, but it is slow.
May produce hypokalemia, hypocalcemia and cerebral vasoconstriction.
Treatment focuses on correcting the cause and controlling ventilation.

pathophysiology: Lower CO₂ reduces carbonic acid concentration, raising pH.
The kidneys attempt to compensate by excreting HCO₃⁻, but take hours‑days.
risk_factors: Hypoxia, heart failure or obstructive lung disease.
signs_symptoms: Numbness and tingling in hands and face.
Dizziness, confusion or seizures in severe cases.
diagnostics: Arterial blood gases: pH 7.46‑7.55, PaCO₂ <35 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ normal or slightly low.
Arterial oxygen (PaO₂) usually normal or elevated.
ECG: may show arrhythmias from hypokalemia.
treatment: Identify and treat the underlying cause (anxiety, pain, fever).
Electrolyte replacement: potassium and calcium orally or IV as needed.
Supplemental oxygen only if hypoxemia is present.
complications: Cerebral vasoconstriction → decreased blood flow and possible syncope.
Respiratory decompensation if the underlying cause worsens.
nursing_care: Monitor arterial blood gases every 2‑4 h until stabilization.
Assess signs of electrolyte imbalance (ECG, muscle weakness).
Teach slow, deep breathing; semi‑Fowler position.
Record respiratory rate, heart rate and O₂ saturation.
patient_teaching: Practice diaphragmatic breathing techniques to avoid hyperventilation.
Recognize symptoms of electrolyte imbalance and seek help.
Maintain adequate hydration and follow a potassium‑rich diet (banana, papaya).
Inform healthcare provider about anxiety or intense pain episodes.

outcomes: NOC: Electrolyte balance – maintain K⁺ ≥3.5 mEq/L
NOC: Neurological status – absence of paresthesias

interventions.action: Monitor serum K⁺ and Ca²⁺ levels every 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Detect electrolyte imbalances that can cause arrhythmias.

interventions.action: Administer potassium or calcium supplements as prescribed.
Evaluate ECG at least once daily or if palpitations occur.
interventions.rationale: Identify arrhythmias related to electrolyte disturbances.

interventions.action: Teach the patient controlled breathing techniques.

outcomes: NOC: Activity tolerance – patient completes daily activities without dyspnea

interventions.action: Assess activity level and record vital signs before and after.
Plan rest periods every 10‑15 min during activities.
Apply diaphragmatic breathing techniques during exertion.
interventions.rationale: Improve ventilation and reduce shortness of breath.

interventions.action: Collaborate with physical therapy for a graded exercise program.
interventions.rationale: Gradually increase aerobic capacity and tolerance.

interventions.action: Educate the patient on the importance of avoiding hyperventilation during exercise.
interventions.rationale: Maintain PaCO₂ within normal ranges and prevent alkalosis.

summary.0.quote: Acute asthma exacerbations, pulmonary embolisms, or other respiratory disorders can initially cause respiratory alkalosis as the lungs breathe faster in an attempt to increase oxygenation, which decreases the PaCO 2 .

key_points.0.quote: Anxiety, pain, fear, asthma exacerbation, pulmonary embolus Hyperventilation Respiratory alkalosis (pH >7.45; PaCO 2 <35 mm Hg) Hypoventilation in response to alka

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: Acute asthma exacerbations, pulmonary embolisms, or other respiratory disorders can initially cause respiratory alkalosis as the lungs breathe faster in an attempt to increase oxygenation, which decreases the PaCO 2 .

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Hyperventilation can occur due to anxiety, panic attacks, pain, fear, head injuries, or mechanical ventilation .

sections.diagnostics.2.quote: A specific type of hypoxia is hypoxemia , defined as decreased partial pressure of oxygen in the blood (PaO 2 ) indicated in an ABG result.

sections.treatment.0.quote: Hyperventilation can occur due to anxiety, panic attacks, pain, fear, head injuries, or mechanical ventilation .

sections.complications.3.quote: As hypoxia worsens, the patient’s level of consciousness and vital signs will worsen with an increased respiratory rate and heart rate and decreased pulse oximetry readings.

sections.nursing_care.3.quote: Respiration is a critical function and is included as one of the vital signs, which most commonly include respiratory rate, heart rate, temperature, and blood pressure.
